title: Let Kids Try to Solve Their Own Problems, Say Experts
paragraphs: In an age when answers to almost any question are just a click away, many parents are quick to step in when their children face a problem. But according to developmental experts and educators, letting children struggle a little may actually help them develop important skills.

Experts say that problem-solving is a skill that has to be practiced. Dr. Dana Suskind, a professor of surgery and pediatrics at the University of Chicago and the author of the book "Human Raised," argues that the most important thing adults can give children is not the answer, but the experience of figuring it out. According to Suskind, when parents rush to solve problems, children miss out on chances to practice skills such as pausing before acting, remembering what worked in the past and trying new solutions.

Other experts warn of longer-term effects. Dr. Stephanie Carlson, the director of the Institute of Child Development at the University of Minnesota, says that children who rarely struggle may feel severe anxiety when they eventually have to solve problems on their own. Kiryn Hoffman, the CEO of the National Children's Museum in Washington, D.C., adds that even boredom can encourage creativity and help children build confidence and resilience.

Some parents are already putting these ideas into practice. Nicole Knoth, a mother of two teenage girls in Arizona, gave her daughters $5 at a store when they were five years old and let them work out what they could afford. Today, her daughters do the grocery shopping, and the oldest manages her own credit card.

So how can parents help? Experts suggest pausing before stepping in. When the stakes are low, parents can talk problems through with their children using open-ended questions, such as "What do you think?" or "How could you solve this?" However, when there is a real danger, parents should step in.

Experts also stress that every child is different, so parents need to consider their child's age, maturity and circumstances before giving them more independence. Independence also does not mean doing everything alone. For example, a child who realizes they do not understand a math problem and asks a teacher for help is also practicing an important skill.
